passage:
Week three in Hyderabad. Sabina lived alone in a one-room flat, worked from home and ordered groceries online. She hadn't hugged anyone in a month. She felt restless and flat at once. When the vegetable seller's hand touched hers while giving change, she had to look away because her throat went tight.
Week five. She called her sister Sunaina. "I feel so silly. I just miss being touched. Even a pat on the back."
"That's not silly. That's human," Sunaina said. "Find people. A class, a group, anything."
That weekend Sabina joined a Sunday pottery class at the community centre. The teacher guided her hands on the wheel.
Week eight. Sunaina visited. At the station they hugged for a long time. That night Sabina had plans with two women from pottery. The flat felt less empty.

qa.q: What class did Sabina join?
qa.a: She joined a Sunday pottery class at the community centre.

qa.q: How was Sabina feeling in week three?
qa.a: She felt restless, flat and lonely, so much that a brief touch from the vegetable seller made her throat tight.

qa.q: What choice helped Sabina meet her need for contact safely?
qa.a: Calling her sister and joining the pottery class, which brought friends and warm company.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt hearing Sabina say she felt silly?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt caring and protective, wanting her sister to know her feelings were normal.

grounding: It shows a person living alone growing restless, low and sensitive without friendly touch, and meeting that need through family and community.

passage:
Shankar, you've been looking lonely since the transfer. Let me tell you a story. When I was your age, the company posted me to a dam site in the hills for eight months. I lived alone in a tin quarter. No phone, just letters.
By the third month I was a mess. Bored, snappy, lying awake. When the cook's little boy grabbed my hand to show me a beetle, I nearly wept. I hadn't realised how much I missed a simple touch.
That was the turning point. I started eating with the cook's family instead of alone. I joined the Sunday cricket with the site workers, all back-slaps and shoulder-grabs. The cook's wife would thump my back and say, "Eat more, Zubin-bhai."
I stopped lying awake. So go to that office badminton evening. Don't sit alone.

qa.q: How long was Zubin posted at the dam site?
qa.a: Zubin was posted there for eight months.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when the cook's boy grabbed Zubin's hand?
qa.a: Zubin was so moved as to nearly weep, realising how much simple touch had been missing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Zubin's story, and what changed after it?
qa.a: The boy grabbing Zubin's hand; after that Zubin ate with the cook's family and joined Sunday cricket, finding warm company.

qa.q: How might the cook's family have seen the young Zubin?
qa.a: They probably saw a lonely young man far from home and welcomed Zubin like family.

grounding: It shows a person living alone for weeks growing restless and low without friendly touch, and finding safe company in a community.

passage: Pooja, twenty-five, had moved to Bhubaneswar for her new job in June, and then the monsoon arrived and never seemed to leave. Offices went online. She lived alone in a one-room flat, and for six weeks she hadn't touched another person or had a real conversation. She felt restless and low, scrolling late, crying at silly advertisements. One day the vegetable seller squeezed her hand as he gave her change, and she had to turn away, eyes stinging. That evening her brother Hemant video-called. 'You look terrible, Pooja.' She told him the truth. 'I think I'm just lonely.' 'Of course you are. That's human, not weak.' He helped her find a weekend choir at the community hall. The first Saturday, a woman beside her linked arms as they sang, and Pooja felt something inside her unclench.

qa.q: Where did Pooja move for her new job?
qa.a: To Bhubaneswar.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel after six weeks alone?
qa.a: She felt restless, low and lonely, crying at silly advertisements.

qa.q: What healthy step did Hemant help Pooja take?
qa.a: Joining a weekend choir at the community hall, where she could meet people.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt seeing Pooja on the video call?
qa.a: He was probably worried and concerned for his sister, and wanted to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult living alone who becomes restless, low and sensitive after weeks without company, and finds community to meet the need for comfort.

passage: Thomas, twenty-six, worked from his flat in Kochi. His parents were in Dubai, his friends had scattered after college, and some weeks he spoke to no one except on video calls. He noticed he was restless in the evenings, pacing, snapping at the delivery boy for being late. When his neighbour Akash knocked to borrow a screwdriver, Thomas talked to him for forty minutes and felt ridiculous afterwards. Then Akash knocked again the next week. 'A few of us play badminton at the church hall on Tuesdays. Come?' Thomas went. They shook hands, clapped each other on the back after rallies, went for chai after. On the walk home, Thomas realised his shoulders weren't tense. He started going every Tuesday, and to Sunday lunch at Akash's family flat once a month.

qa.q: What did Akash come to borrow?
qa.a: A screwdriver.

qa.q: How had Thomas been feeling living alone?
qa.a: He had been restless, lonely and irritable, snapping at the delivery boy.

qa.q: What helped Thomas meet his need for company?
qa.a: Badminton with neighbours on Tuesdays, chai afterwards, and monthly Sunday lunch at Akash's family flat.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Thomas talked for forty minutes?
qa.a: Akash may have sensed that Thomas was lonely and felt friendly enough to invite him out.

grounding: Shows a young adult living alone feeling restless and low after weeks without company or friendly touch, and finding community to meet that need.

passage:
'Jahnavi, you've been crying since you walked in.'
'I know. Sorry, Pooja. It's stupid.'
'Tell me.'
'I got my hair cut today. The barber put her hand on my head to tilt it, and I nearly burst into tears. Nobody's touched me in, like, a month.'
'Since you moved out?'
'Since the lockdown at work, working from home. I live alone. I talk to my plants.'
'That's not stupid. That's lonely.'
Jahnavi nodded, wiping her face.
'Can I hug you?'
'Please.'
Pooja held her for a long moment. 'Right. Sunday lunches at my place. Every week. And you're joining my running group.'
Jahnavi laughed, still teary. 'You're bossy.'
'I know.'

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say she talks to at home?
qa.a: Her plants.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when the barber touched her head?
qa.a: She felt a sudden lonely ache, nearly bursting into tears after a month without friendly touch.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that met Jahnavi's need in a healthy way?
qa.a: She asked before hugging, then offered weekly Sunday lunches and her running group.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel hearing that Jahnavi has been alone for a month?
qa.a: Pooja probably feels sad and protective, wanting to include Jahnavi more.

grounding: Shows a young adult living alone who has become sensitive and low after weeks without touch, and a friend offering welcome comfort and regular company.

passage: The winter I moved to Chandigarh for a remote job, I went nineteen days without any friendly touch. I only noticed because the pharmacist's hand brushed mine while giving me change, and I nearly cried at the counter. I'm Nikita, and I'd always thought of myself as someone who liked being alone. But that month I was restless, sleeping badly, snapping at my own reflection and tearing up at dog-food adverts. I felt silly for wanting a hug so much. Then my old college friend Asif, who lived across town, messaged about a Sunday cycling group. I went. Afterwards eight of us sat on the grass eating chole kulche, knees bumping, and someone clapped me on the back. I also started calling Mummy every night. Nothing magic. But I stopped feeling like a ghost.

qa.q: How many days did Nikita go without any friendly touch?
qa.a: Nineteen days.

qa.q: Why did Nikita nearly cry at the pharmacy counter?
qa.a: Nikita felt lonely and starved of contact, so even a brush of a hand felt overwhelming.

qa.q: Which safe ways did Nikita find to meet the need for contact?
qa.a: Joining Asif's Sunday cycling group, sharing food on the grass with others, and calling Mummy every night.

qa.q: What might Asif have noticed when Nikita joined the cycling group?
qa.a: Asif may have been glad to see an old friend come out and join in, perhaps without knowing how lonely Nikita had been.

grounding: Shows a person living alone growing restless, low and sensitive after weeks without friendly touch, and meeting the need safely through friends, family and community.
